speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say we enjoyed listening to that exhaustive examination of the proposed changes to the rules of the House. Now, of course, we are debating government motion No. 30, rules of the House of Commons and changes to the Standing Orders.
It sounds very straightforward and perhaps rather inconsequential in many respects to those listening to the debates and watching the discussions. Thirty pages in our books, 64 different clauses. Let's face it, there is quite a range of issues here, some very trivial issues that simply needed to be brought up to date in terms of the modernization of dealing with the legislative material.
Others have touches of totalitarianism associated with them, major changes in terms of how the House of Commons operates.
Perhaps it is not by mistake. You will notice how it is dark over the House of Commons today. When you look out the windows there is a dark cloud hanging over the House of Commons. It is symbolic, I might add, in terms of the dark cloud that hangs over the Parliament of Canada and the dark cloud, indeed, that is hanging over parliamentary democracy as we know it in this country.
I must say that what we are debating today is perhaps one of the most important issues that we will debate in this House for the next number of weeks and months. Today, when the Prime Minister introduced the President of Mexico, he referred to the House of Commons as the "crucible of parliamentary democracy". When the President of Mexico spoke, he referred to this House as "the House of democracy in which is determined the will of the people of Canada".
April 8, 1991

This is a crucial House of debate. This is where the duly elected representatives of the people of Canada come to reflect the views of their constituents and reflect their views as elected people regarding government policy and government programs. We were asked to study and to examine these government policies, programs and proposals, to examine their impact on different regions of the country and on different groups within our society, whether it was the free trade agreement or the goods and services tax. I refer to these as perhaps two of the largest and most important pieces of legislation we have had a chance to discuss in this House in the past number of months.
I think all of us, certainly the people of Canada, would recognize that it is very important we debate issues that the government of the day brings forward and that we examine legislation in detail, that we hold the government accountable for its deeds or for its actions or for the various acts of individual cabinet ministers. We have seen over the past number of months, as a result of that accountability, whole sets of ministers of the cabinet have had to resign or have seen fit to resign.
The government House leader spoke of the anger and frustration of the electorate and the fact that they hold members of Parliament or politicians, generally, in contempt. May I suggest that one of the many reasons for that is that people feel a sense of powerlessness. They have strong views on certain issues, whether it is the GST or the free trade agreement, and they bring it to their members of Parliament. They raise their issues at parliamentary committees or through other avenues, and the government totally ignores them.
When a government House leader says that it is important for members of Parliament to go back to listen to their constituents, we all know that constituents have been saying to members of the government for months and months on end: "Do not proceed with the goods and services tax", in every constituency across the country. Those of us in opposition have risen to reflect the views of our constituents. Many of us on dozens and dozens, and perhaps hundreds of occasions, have reflected their views that this tax is punitive, cruel and mean and is the wrong tax to be bringing in at this time.
Government Orders
I look across the aisle and I know that some of my friends on the government benches hold meetings in their constituencies and they are publicized. The media attends and reflects the mood of the constituents and the questions being raised. Once again, hundreds of thousands of people have registered their opposition to the goods and services tax or to the free trade agreement or to the changes to the unemployment insurance legislation, and the government just ignores their concerns.
They are not listening.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
No wonder people are frustrated. No wonder the electorate feels that the government does not care, because it has not shown in any way, shape or form that they, in fact, do care about what the people who elected them are concerned about.
I think people are saying that they are fed up with government arrogance. What they call this government, essentially, is an elected dictatorship, where the government is elected for a period of time and it feels it has the mandate to do anything it wishes. It does not matter that the programs and policies it is introducing was not discussed or raised during the last federal campaign.
As a matter of fact, I think it was the present Minister for International Trade who said, not many weeks before the last campaign that: "We could not tell the people of Canada what we were going to do, because if we did, no one would elect us". So, obviously, they fooled the people of Canada. They did not say: "If we are elected, we are going to introduce the goods and services tax".
So when the government House leader says that Parliament must be reformed, I must say that we can have all the rules in the world and unless the will is there, it is not going to change behaviour. We know that as parliamentarians. We can have all the rules and regulations of the House, but unless there is a will to make this place work properly, it will not work properly. We know that as parents. You can have all the rules for your children that you want, but unless there is a will, if you like, to do the appropriate thing, to act appropriately, to conduct your business in ways according to accepted traditions, it does not take place.
That is why I say, if the government is hoping that this type of parliamentary reform they are now introducing, and will eventually jam through the House of Commons, because again they will have to use the heavy hand of closure to get their way.

April 8, 1991
Government Orders
This is not going to change the situation if the government continues to ignore the people of Canada. What we see month after month and year after year, we hear people speaking out. Why is it so critical that we have an opportunity to discuss these issues in depth?
I want to use one example. When the government brought in the idea that we should de-index pensions, it said: "We should de-index the pensions of all those people who collect old age security." In other words, we should erode those pensions over time.
The opposition said: "We have got to let the people of Canada know what this is going to do. We have to let pensioners and future pensioners know what the impact of this legislation is all about." We debated the issue day after day, and slowly the people of Canada recognized what the government was attempting to do. It was going to erode the pension system of Canada, and the people spoke out.
The Prime Minister, to give him credit, said that the government was wrong, that it should not have done that. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, under these new rules with the government's ability to move legislation through quickly, the people of Canada would not have a chance to react, those pensions would have been de-indexed and the pensioners of this country would see their pensions erode.
That is why we say we want the opportunity to examine legislation, to study it and to invite experts and other people from the outside to come in and look at the government's plans.
I do not think the government is reforming the parliamentary system. It is deforming the parliamentary system to allow it to impose its political agenda on the people of Canada that much more quickly. That is what it is doing.
The government wants to turn this into some sort of sausage factory, not a legislative assembly but a legislative assembly line that just moves legislation through and does not give people a chance to examine it. It does not want to give the opposition a chance to study it. It does not want to provide the same opportunities to hold the government accountable during Question Period.
It is no mistake that it is called Question Period. All we hear are the questions. We never get any answers back. This is one way we have of bringing to the people's attention what the government is doing. I hate to say it, but as a result of questioning in this House of Commons, one after another, cabinet ministers have had to resign their seats: One, two, three, four, five, six. It goes on and on.
It would not have happened if we had not had a chance to raise questions during Question Period concerning a minister's behaviour. Now we are going to see that erode as the government attempts to do away with Question Period for certain times of the year.
The government House leader went on at some length to explain why it is appropriate that members of Parliament get home to listen to their constituents. I pointed that that argument is rather hollow. Obviously the track record would speak for itself that this government does not listen to people. The members can go home every day of the year and nothing will change.
The point is that when their constituents tell them what to do or what not to do, the constituents know they will be totally and simply ignored.
There is another aspect of this. It was pointed out to me by my colleague from Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing, who I want to say at this point has been extremely helpful. His wisdom and the thought that went into this process has to be recognized by all as leading to some very meaningful discussion inside and outside our caucus in terms of the changes being proposed to the government and essentially what they will do. He pointed out to me the other day that the political landscape of this country is changing.
What this government does through these changes is perpetuate the two-party system. We tried to make the case during our so-called negotiations that there are now other viable parties in the House of Commons. The New Democratic Party, a newly elected party, ought to have some recognition in terms of the rule changes, but that was essentially ignored.
We have seen changes introduced to attempt to block small political parties from playing a role in the House of Commons. I refer to the new definition that the government House leader has of unanimous consent. Until
April 8, 1991

now, we had to seek unanimous consent to change the rules at will, virtually.
Sometimes, and as a matter of fact often, it was to the benefit of the House that we alter a rule for a particular afternoon or we change a way of doing business to facilitate a piece of legislation or to assist members in the performance of their duties. The government has changed that. What unanimous consent means is unanimous all but 25 members, so that during Routine Proceedings the government can introduce a motion to pass a bill at all stages or to change the Constitution or to carry out all sorts of what could be termed Draconian changes. Unless 25 members leap to their feet immediately, it is done, just like that. It can be used and abused so easily, but again it will enable the government to facilitate introducing its political agenda through the House of Commons.
I know the government always says: "We have to become more efficient. We have to become more effective". It was very frustrated when the opposition spoke against the goods and services tax and tried to point out why this was the wrong tax. The government was very frustrated when we spoke out against the major changes to the unemployment insurance legislation that would do irreparable harm to families, particularly in the regions of the country. The government was frustrated when we spoke out against the free trade agreement. It said we take too much time talking in the House of Commons.
We appreciate that democracy is not always the most efficient way of doing business. The parliamentary system is not the most effective and efficient way of conducting government business. The most effective way is a dictatorship. That is the most effective way. That is the most business-like way; simply impose the legislation and Parliament is nothing but a rubber stamp if it exists at all.
That is why some of us have felt so strongly about these changes, because that is the direction in which we are moving, where the government simply says: "Here is our agenda". There will be no vote at first reading of a bill. We are going to pass this in principle and put it into a legislative committee where we cannot take time to discuss the bill in any sort of depth. We can only discuss technical aspects.
Government Orders
Mr. Speaker, that would mean that the GST legislation would be introduced, sent off to a committee and unless you were a tax accountant or a tax lawyer, you would not be welcome. You could not call witnesses to say how is this going to affect the farm community, the fishing community; how this is going to affect various sectors of the economy or other elements of society. Oh, no, Mr. Speaker, you could not talk about that. You have to talk about specific details of the legislation.
This is something that we do not support. We think this is wrong. What it means is that rather than the people of Canada, through their organizations, groups or individuals having input into legislation, lobbyists will have input into legislation. They will be the ones who are able to advise the government members and their officials. The people of Canada will be frozen out of the process. That is one of the many reasons why we say we cannot support this package.
The government House leader said that we consented in some way to these rule changes, that he felt that somehow we had agreed during the process that these were acceptable. I think my hon. friend who spoke on behalf of the Official Opposition indicated that that was not the case. It is a bit like being sentenced to death and saying: "Let us negotiate how this is done". We could determine that it could be done by hanging, it could be done by injection or there are a variety of ways to do this.
That is essentially what happened. The government said: "Here are all the changes we want to make so that this place will be more effective, more efficient and more business-like", to run more like a corporate boardroom as opposed to a parliamentary democracy. We said: "We cannot accept these". There are some changes that we can accept. There are some that are rather trivial and simply reflect a changing House of Commons, but there are some measures that we simply cannot accept.
For example, supply days are one of the most important aspects of our work here. Supply days go back to when the king wanted money, he had to set aside certain days to discuss on the part of the duly elected people whether this was an appropriate expenditure or not. We have those days. We have 25 of those each year. We are required to have at least 25 days where the government schedules a day for debate on whether the government is using taxpayers' money adequately and whether their plans are appropriate in terms of more expenditures.

April 8, 1991
Government Orders
It is a long-stated tradition that 25 days during every calendar year be set aside to discuss how the government is spending our money. Now I know the government is doing away with days to debate the budget and the throne speech, and so on. We could talk about those. However, what this one measure does is that it enables the government, if it ever wished, to have the Parliament of Canada sit for only one day a year. What it says is that when we do not sit, those normal supply days will be eroded, will be just ignored. If the government chose not to sit, other than for just one or two days of the year, that is it. There is nothing in the Standing Orders that could change that.
Mr. Speaker, you have signalled that I have one minute left. This is part of the problem. I notice that the government House leader spoke for an hour. The representative of the Official Opposition spoke for an hour and a half, and the New Democratic Party speaks for 20 minutes. That is it.
Does this reflect the true nature of the House of Commons? No, it does not. It reflects an old-fashioned view of the House of Commons where there are two political parties. Mr. Speaker, does this reflect the emerging political reality in the country where we might have four or five or six political parties represented in this House after the next federal election? No. It is just going back in time. That is why we feel this is inappropriate and I simply want to conclude by saying the following.
The government believes that by introducing these changes, which I say tend towards fascism, and I use that term consciously, where the government House leader and the Prime Minister will have the tools now to more effectively muzzle the opposition, to more effectively muzzle the free press, because they too depend on Question Period. That is the only time they have access to the Prime Minister when he dashes up the stairs. He does not call press conferences, and so on.
If the government believes that by imposing these new changes that will severely restrict the opposition members of the House of Commons from doing what they are expected to do on behalf of their constituents, that this is going to allow them to fool the Canadian people sufficiently so that it will be re-elected, it will not work. It will not work. The people of Canada know that this government is not operating with their best interests at heart. They know that this government, after years and years of experience ignores their calls, their pleas. I would say
this is a dark day for the democratic system in this country. It is a dark day for the Parliament of Canada, and that is why we in the New Democratic Party feel that these rules cannot be approved and supported in this House.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have been listening to a rather familiar refrain about dark days. For somebody with such a light head, that is really quite a comment to make.
The hon. member was speaking of muzzling and the high-falutin, high-sounding words on the other side, how all members of Parliament are important and it is important for each one of us to have our opportunity in the House. Then he condemns a package which says that more members will have more opportunities to speak in this House, and that is what the package says.
Let us come to the guts of a test for the member opposite. The members in this House who are muzzled during Question Period sit on this side of the House. Of the 158 of them, 120 do not sit in the cabinet. They get an average of five or six questions a week, to 60 on the other side, for a group that is smaller. If he believes in the principles he has been espousing, will he stand up in this House at this time and adopt the system that exists in Australia, the system that exists in England, where questions go back and forth across the House and all members are treated equally and one side is not expected to be muzzled. Will he agree to that principle?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems odd that we are now getting into a discussion of what the Standing Orders ought to be. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, as has already been proposed, that this be referred to the appropriate standing committee before it is closured off and jammed through the House of Commons. This is the kind of situation that ought to be discussed. My hon. friend is sitting there screaming at me now. That is the appropriate response, presumably, in terms of the government. It cannot handle any kind of criticism.
The point is the following: So-called negotiations never did take place. The member is now suggesting that there are all sorts of changes that we ought to be discussing. I could not agree more. He also knows that the idea was that standing committees ought to be spending more time in pre-study of proposed legislation. That is not in the Standing Orders. These are simply discussions that we have heard.
April 8, 1991

If we were doing the correct thing, and if he really believes that these changes were to make this institution more effective, it would be appropriate then to have more people brought into the process, but the process that was followed was in secret. People were not involved in an open way. This is why I say some of us have offered to the government the suggestion that this be referred to the appropriate standing committee where all the committees are represented in the open, with nothing to hide, and to discuss ways and means of making this more effective.
Again, the old approach, a handful of people in a back room operating in secret is somehow the best way to proceed. I say it is not.
I should use this opportunity, while I am on my feet, to move a subamendment.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order please. If I am not mistaken, the Standing Orders do not allow a member to move an amendment during the period for questions and comments.
I therefore remind the hon. member that we are still in that period.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: A supplementary, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On a point of order, the hon. member for Edmonton East.

Mr. Speaker, might I suggest you inquire of the House as to whether or not there is unanimous consent to allow the House leader to propose his amendment and, in the spirit of the proposed amendments to Standing Orders, see if there are fewer than 25 members who object.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up with a brief supplementary and we will follow another one of his suggestions. The first principle was muzzling, the second principle was freedom of expression in the Chamber. It is so easy to follow through on his principles
Government Orders
that I simply say to the member, let us have unanimous consent to continue this debate until midnight tonight so that we could all have a better chance to talk about it. I am asking for unanimous consent to continue the debate until midnight, to follow through on his principles. Does he want freedom of speech or does he not?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Does the House give unanimous consent to extend the-

Mr. Speaker, further to the amendments on the changes to the Standing Orders of the House, I would like to make a comment to the hon. member. We must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that the government worked for months on this with the opposition; there are no surprises for anyone in this House. The opposition can hardly be surprised by anything in this package. What we see is its biased reaction to what is a good reform that will make Parliament more effective and bring it closer to the people. That is what Canadians want.
I think that it is important for a member from a large region like Abitibi, which is 555,000 square kilometres to be in Ottawa for three weeks and in my riding for one week. It is important for Northerners, for a member from a region like mine, to be in the riding at least one week a month. Earlier, the member said that the government wanted to do away with Question Period. I will give you an example of what democracy is. Today, during Question Period, I was scheduled to ask the Hon. Minister Benoit Bouchard a question through the Speaker of the House of Commons.
I was unable to do so. You had the opportunity during that period to ask several questions. As a member of the government party from a large region like the Abitibi, it is important for members from large regions to be there one week a month. In this House, we often notice,

Government Orders
although you are present a month at a time, that half your colleagues are never in Parliament.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

speakeroldname: Mr. Benno Friesen (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been following this debate not simply for the two or three hours just passed, but over the many years that I have been in the House along with some of my colleagues here from Newfoundland and so forth. We have taken a great deal of interest over the years.
When I first came here in 1974 I remember very clearly the attitude that some of the members at that time still had about the revised rules of the House brought in in 1969,1 believe it was, which varied the rules
considerably. To them it was still convulsive to think about the radical changes that were brought in such as having opposition days instead of committee of the whole for a lot of the bills, especially the money bills.
Change is always very difficult, but I want to begin by complimenting the House leader for the Liberal Party on the contribution he has made to the debate today. I thought he spoke and contributed very well to an understanding of the issues that are before us. He did it dispassionately and as much as it can be done in the Chamber like this, and we cannot always absent ourselves from partisanship, he did it at a very high level. I want to compliment him for that. I cannot say the same thing for the House leader of the New Democratic Party.
I think we ought to assign someone here to keep a box score of the number of cliches the member for Kamloops can throw about in one of his 10 or 20-minute speeches. The degree to which he banters them about is almost beyond counting. It is worthy to note that while he spoke in his address about the need for further debate, the muzzling of Parliament, and all of those cliches that roll so quickly off his tongue, when we gave him the opportunity to extend the debate so that his members could take part, he said: "No, we don't want to extend the debate. We just want to talk about the way Parliament has been muzzled". Give them a chance to talk and they say "no".
We have had a further display of this. I noted that one of the things that the New Democratic Party is opposed to is the fact that we want to change the times when the House is sitting. We would have one week a month away from the House when we could do constituency work. They do not like that idea. The fact is that in reality, they are already on a platoon system. They are already doing it. They are off in their ridings one week out of the month.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
They do not want to give that privilege any kind of official endorsement. They want to do it quietly so that nobody notices.
I noticed, particularly this morning, when that party which is so interested in developing countries had an opportunity to support the president of a developing country like Mexico, it had 15 members here this morning, I counted; 35 per cent of its caucus was here, 65 per cent was somewhere else. Yet, when that party ran

That is right.
April 8, 1991

for election it said: "We want to represent you in Ottawa".
Do not throw stones in a glass house. How many were you missing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That brings me to the real dilemma which all members of Parliament confront. All of us, when we stand for election, when we go through an election campaign, face this dilemma. In one way or another we are saying to our constituents: "I want to represent you in Ottawa". We say it regardless of party. We say it with all sincerity, and we want to do this. We want to go to Ottawa and take the needs and the concerns and the issues of our people and give them voice here in this Chamber.
I remember toward the end of my first campaign, an elector, an elderly gentleman said to me, talking about all of the candidates: "The trouble with you guys is that once we elect you, we never see you again". Prior to, and in the 1950s and 1960s that was almost unavoidable. Travel was by train. The person elected took the train from Vancouver to Ottawa, spent three months in Ottawa and then came. Obviously, the geography of the country determines that once they are elected it is not going to be very often that you will see that member again. Geography is one of the difficulties of representing a constituency in Canada. That is a dilemma we all face. It has nothing to do with party affiliation. It has nothing to do with ideology. It has entirely to do with geography.
So, we are caught in that dilemma. We want to represent our people in Ottawa and yet we also want to be with our people in the constituency.
I want to say to members opposite that this formula was dear to my heart when I sat on opposition benches, because it is important for us to speak out for our constituencies in Ottawa and represent them well here. At the same time, it is also important for us to be back home to get an understanding and a feel for what our constituents are saying.
One of the truisms of life is that the longer you spend in Ottawa, the more unrealistic the world becomes to you. It is only as we go back to our constituencies and only as we spend time with people who elected us, that we maintain a realistic view of what Canada is all about, what life is all about. The longer we stay in this city consistently, without any break, the surer we are of getting an unrealistic perspective of issues here and in
Government Orders
our constituencies, and of our responsibilities. It is only as we go back home that we become reconnected to reality and understand the issues.
When I was in opposition, I was already in favour of this kind of reform. Added to that, I could see that the ministers of the Crown sitting in the treasury benches had an additional responsibility. They had an administrative responsibility that I, as a backbencher did not have. Yet management is a very important facet of government business.
Here are the ministers of the Crown-and again it does not matter which party is in office. Here is a minister of the Crown who has to be at Question Period every day and has to spend time being briefed for Question Period. At the same time he is concerned about his department, how it is being managed. The more time he spends here for Question Period, the more he is turning over to bureaucrats the management of the department. He has less time to examine what the bureaucrats are doing.
I heard recently that one of the ministers of the Crown had the highest compliment given to him when his department said "he is the best deputy minister we have ever had". By that it meant that this person is involved with every concern in his department. That is not always possible if you are trying to divide your time between the House and, as the opposition rightly demands, accounting for the administration which, in fact, includes administering and managing the department.
The opposition says that if you reduce the time you spend in the chamber you reduce the amount of democracy. Now, I think that deserves a little bit of examination:
I would contend that this is certainly an important forum for democracy but it does not begin here. Democracy really begins on the campaign trail, on the election trail, when we are elected to office. During that time we espouse the platforms we would promote if we were elected to office. I have said this on a number of occasions here. This is an idea that comes from the parties of the mother of Parliaments over in the United Kingdom. The platform, what they call the party manifesto, is all important. When they are campaigning they have a very carefully structured party manifesto and a platform which they enunciate during the campaign, and when they are elected they are accountable for making

April 8, 1991
Government Orders
sure that the legislative program that they introduce as a government follows their party manifesto.
Now that is the first step of democracy.
So when are you going to start using it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I will come to that.
Never.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If we allow campaigning, as we have in the past, to be nothing but sloganeering, like "the land is strong" or "zap, you are frozen", if slogans which have very little to do with your legislative program once you are elected dominate your campaign, you will diminish the level of democracy right at the threshold where it ought to begin. When we diminish it there, naturally when we get into the Chamber here we have a free rein. If there is no structure in the campaign it is no wonder then that when you get to the Chamber opposition parties will object to the program that the government is presenting; it has had no forerunner, it has had no foundation.
Democracy begins on the campaign trail, and then it is developed here in, as someone said, "the crucible of democracy".
Therefore, to reduce the number of sitting days but lengthen the hours so that you have an aggregate number of increased hours is not a reduction of democracy. That is making democracy work.
I remember in the campaign of 1984 our party very clearly talked about wanting to dismantle the national energy program, and yet as soon as we were elected and we started doing that we were opposed. I mean, this is something we promised to do and yet the opposition said "you don't have a right to do what you promised to do".
Then we proposed, during the election campaign, privatization of the government corporations and the opposition said "no, no, you can't do that", but we had promised to do it.
It seems to me that is what an election campaign is all about. I come back to the United Kingdom experience. There is a saying over there among the two or three opposing parties-whatever the year happens to be- that the government is entitled to its legislation. It does,
it gets it as it ought to. The opposition is entitled to debate what it sees as the flaws of that concept, of that ideology. That is true. That is the opposition's right and it ought to be exercised.
In the United Kingdom-and my friend from Newfoundland walks out-they debate an issue like that for five, six or seven not weeks, not days, but hours for a bill of some magnitude. They have concluded that if the government has campaigned on a platform and it was elected to introduce its platform and to legislate it into being, it is entitled to do that.
I remember sitting here for hours at night debating a bill on which we had campaigned, and we were being told withdraw the bill after we had campaigned on it. Somehow that to me sounds like a contradiction to democracy.
In the 1984 campaign we had over 50 per cent of the vote. Presumably we had a right to do it. That did not stop the opposition. Now the leader of the government says 53 per cent voted against us in the 1988 campaign. Well I do not remember any time when the Liberals were elected when they had 50 per cent of the vote. That did not stop them from introducing their election campaign platform, their legislation. They did what they wanted even though they had less than 50 per cent of the vote.
I want to point out that the beginning of democracy having a clearly defined campaign, that the crucible of democracy is here and we are entitled to legislate the campaign promises that we introduced and we go on from there.
I would like to underline another concept and that is the myth that by reducing the number of days we are introducing a radical new reduction of democracy when, as the government House leader pointed out this morning, Australia with a geography somewhat problematic to them, like we have here, has 66 sitting days a year. It passes 89 per cent of the bills introduced. Canada sits 155 days, two and a half times as long, and passes 56 per cent of the bills introduced.
I am asking members opposite: is that an efficient use of parliamentary time? If we have campaigned on a platform and the legislation flows from it, are we not
April 8, 1991

entitled as an efficient democratic body to introduce and receive passage of that legislation?
West Germany sits on the average of 17 days a year. It passes 90 per cent of its legislation. Japan sits 43 days a year and passes 76 per cent of its bills. Even the United States, which has a little bit of a problem of geography and population, sits only 144 days a year and passes the majority of its legislation.
It is a little bit of a ruse to say that by reducing the number of days we sit so that we can spend time in our constituencies but increasing the number of hours in the days we sit so that we maintain the same amount of time in the chamber, is somehow a reduction in democracy.
I want to make one other point and that has to do with Question Period. If members opposite are interested in improving the efficiency of Question Period, I would simply point out to them that they have the same bothersome, meddlesome worries I had when I sat over there: The prima donnas who sit on the front benches hog all the camera time.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have their attention, Mr. Speaker. The man who is best at it is laughing. When you have members sitting in the front and asking questions that take two and three minutes, that inspire answers that are just as long, two or three minutes, give me a break, you cannot have many questions answered in a 45 minute question period. What each caucus needs to do is put the boots to those guys who hog the camera and the time, limit them and get rid of the speeches and ask short, pertinent questions that require short, pertinent answers. We will improve Question Period far more than adding a few days of Question Period to the calendar of the House of Commons.
I invite each caucus, including ours, to do that, then we will improve the procedure of the House of Commons.
Third, I want to talk about committees. Can I speak as long as the opposition House leader did? The third point I want to make is regarding committees. It is important that we start invoking the principle of approval in principle in the House and make committees do the work of technical improvement of the bills.
Government Orders
I remember when we were debating C-55 and C-84. We had an immigration lawyer before us who opposed the bill. He was not in favour of the bill. He came before the committee, not to say withdraw the bill. He said: "You have improved it in principle, now here are ways I think that you can improve it". That is what we need to do.
And you ignored him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We did not. My friend from Spadina said we ignored him. No, we did not. As a matter of fact, he gave us very good consultative advice that we used.
I am sorry I do not have as much time as the opposition House leader. I know the members of the opposition would love to hear me speak longer, but I heed your advice.

Mr. Speaker, speaking for this side of the House, the only ruse in this place is the one being regurgitated by the government here tonight and being roasted by us on this side.
The hon. member speaks well of reality if the reality was that this was the year 1969, because today, in 1991, we have had advancements in communications and the tools of communication, the likes of which this member has not seen in 15 to 20 years. We have the parliamentary reports which we can put out quarterly. Every three months you can send one out. We have access to distribute information in lots of 4,000 pieces, as many times a week as you care to. We have free mailing privileges that go out to all your constituents in your riding.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Community television.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Community television, the Whip for the opposition party states. Community television where you can go and take a member of the government if you want to, if he or she is obliging, and go across the street to a cable organization, sit down with that person, spend 28 minutes discussing the issues of the day and mail it to your riding. Free mailing privileges and telephone privileges. If someone calls or someone expresses a problem to your constituency, you can get on that phone immediately from your constituency office and call that constituent back immediately.

April 8, 1991
Government Orders
I am available to my constituents. All they have to do is call the office and make it a point to tell my office that they want to see me. I say terrific. I am in the House Monday through Friday doing the job in the highest court of the land, the privilege that we have to be here on behalf of our constituents. This is the place of work. If we could move it to Hamilton West we would be more than happy to, but unfortunately there are 295 members with the same opinion. We cannot even convince the government to get an airport there, never mind the House of Commons. They can make it a point to request that they would like to see me on Saturday.
The constituency office is open Saturdays for that express purpose. If we really love this job, if we are really here because we believe in our country and we want to do the right thing for our constituents, if we want to stand up for our home town no matter where it is in this country, we are going to make ourselves available to the people who put us here.
That is what we are being paid for, and that is the job that we are here for.
Right on.

I do not want to test the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley but I want to ask him: "When did the sun rise-"
I will come to my question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Oh, you've got a question?

This is question and comments. I will give my comment, and I will ask the member a question.
This member has been in the House for how many years?
Too long.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Sixteen: it does not matter.
The member has been in the House for 16 years. When did the sun finally rise-
Order, let someone else ask a question.

I am asking a question. When did the sun finally rise on this member that after 16 years, he finds it important that he must be back to his constituency for one week out of four.
It seems that for the last 16 years he has managed to do that quite capably. Did he rise in this House ever in the past 16 years and say: "By golly, Mr. Speaker, I have to get back to my riding association at least one week in four because I cannot seem to get the job done otherwise." No. Sixteen years he sat in this House, and there was no problem.
Now the government comes through with this new edict, this new magic for parliamentary reform which is complete nonsense. It is an appendage like an arm that should be cut off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, here is a man from Hamilton who leaves his office at nine o'clock and can be here at 10.30 a.m. He has no time zone changes.
I will tell you that it is speeches like his that make western Canadians despise central Canada. They hate it with a vengeance.
He can vote here on a Wednesday and be at a meeting Wednesday night in his riding.
I will tell you: I get up and leave Vancouver at 9 a.m. and land here at 4.30 p.m. The day is gone. He can leave his office at 9 a.m. and get here at 10.30 a.m.
Smart aleck, that will never sell. He talks about all the brochures and what have you that he sends to his riding. Fine. So do I. That is why I have been here for 16 years. I do not think he will be here next time with that kind of an attitude.
For all the letters, parliamentary reviews and householders that we send out, the reality is that the people still want to talk to us personally. They want to meet with us personally. It is not easy to do when we have a six-hour flight on a Thursday or Friday. It is not easy to do six hours after a days' work and then meet constituents.
Wake up, smell the coffee and see how big Canada is. I want this member to know, Sir, it is one thing to send out householders and it is another thing to see them in flesh and blood. Maybe his wife is satisfied with a phone call, but I think she would rather see him in person. That is the way constituents feel, too.
It is not enough to get a letter. It is not enough to get a householder that your staff printed. They want to see us. They want to meet with us. For once, I would like to find a central Canadian from that party who would travel to the west often enough to see what it is like to represent a
April 8, 1991

constituency out there and still meet the needs, aspirations and the feelings of those people out there.
Hear, hear.

The question of the proposal with respect to three weeks on, one week off, has been around for a long time. It was looked at by the McGrath committee. It was not rejected at that time on its merits. It seems to me there are good arguments on both sides, and that is not the debate I am here to enter at this point.
I want to speak to what the member actually had to say and some of the things he did not say. He talked about governments having the right to implement their mandates. I agree with him. There is often irony in the questions that opposition members pose, but there are also examples of when governments bring forward things that they did not promise. All governments are guilty of this, and your government has been guilty of this as well, with respect. In my judgement, the GST and the free trade agreement, at least after 1984, are examples. There are times when the opposition feels that the government did not make point of saying it was going to do that, and I think it is legitimate at that point for people to make that part of the debate.
The member mentioned Question Period, which I think has deteriorated seriously in the time that I have been here. I remember when I first came here. Speaker Jerome was in the Chair. People were cut off if they had long preambles or were not permitted supplementaries. I think part of the deterioration of Question Period owes itself to the lack of discipline, with respect, that the Chair is unwilling to impose on the House, and also to the discipline of television, which looks for those 15 or 30-second sound bites which the old Question Period did not provide as easily. We have conformed ourselves to that medium and perhaps we need to take a second look at that.
The member made a point with respect to committees. He knows that when we considered these kinds of things during the McGrath committee, we also considered a process whereby the principle and the substance of bills would be considered beforehand in a way that this particular reform that he is now defending, does not introduce. That is one of the reasons why we are critical of it.
Government Orders
Finally, with respect to the whole question of efficiency, I think you could stand to introduce new efficiencies into this system if you at the same time introduced new meaning into those more efficient processes. This reform has failed to do that. You have not given real meaning and power to the participation of opposition members at the same time as you have introduced new efficiencies. That is where you fall down.
I wonder if the member could tell me why, in his defence, he did not mention the four areas where this reform-or deform, as we have called it-specifically goes back on recommendations made by the McGrath committee of which he was a part. The re-introduction of parliamentary secretaries into the standing committees is a case in point.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The time for questions and comments is over. Does the House give its unanimous consent?
Agreed.

Then there is the question of limited rooms for committees meeting within these envelopes, which will, as sure as I am standing here, have the effect of not permitting all committees to work when they want to work. That will take away the self-initiating power which the McGrath committee recommended. There is the question of legislative versus standing committees and the power which this reform would give to the government to decide whether or not a matter went to a legislative committee or a standing committee. Again, eroding the McGrath reforms. Finally, putting the whole matter of substitution even more under the Whips than it is now, when the spirit of the McGrath committee was to take power away from the Whips and invest it in the private members. The Whips have too much power over this place already. They are a scourge on this place. The essence of the McGrath report was to give more power to the private member, more power to committees, and that is exactly what this reform is not doing. In fact, the reform is going in the opposite direction.
I know I am not being fair in the sense that I have not given him the time to do so, but the member was a member of the McGrath committee and it would have been interesting to hear how he can justify these changes, knowing as I do, the position he held collective-

Adjournment Debate
ly with me and other members in 1985 on these same matters.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 25, the Commissioner of Official Languages submitted his annual report to the House of Commons. Given the social and political, or rather linguistic, climate, this report showed very encouraging signs of the rise of bilingualism in the country. It thus counterbalanced a more negative interim report, in my humble opinion, Mr. Speaker, made public five days earlier by the Spicer Commission on March 20.
In his report, the Commissioner of Official Languages says that four out of five Canadipans accept official bilingualism. Another encouraging fact: three out of four parents want their children to learn the second official language in immersion courses. Mr. Speaker, although this report mentions rising support for bilingualism in Canada, it also denounces the inertia of Treasury Board. The Commissioner says on page 36 and I quote:
The list of what the Treasury Board Secretariat did in 1990 is not half as interesting as the catalogue of what it did not do.
The Commissioner says on page 83:
The Heasury Board should be the engine of the renewal decreed by Parliament. We do not ask that it display zealousness; in future, we would merely ask that it discharge more effectively all its language policy responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, that is why on March 25 I asked the President of the Treasury Board in this House how he could explain the 22 per cent reduction in staff at the Official Languages Division of Treasury Board, his own department. I asked him how he could reduce staff from 64 to 50 in this division which, as we know, is responsible for applying in his department and federal departments a law that is sometimes misunderstood, sometimes mismanaged and often misapplied.
The President of the Treasury Board replied-obviously evading the issue-that this division's budget had increased rather than decreased. Treasury Board is to check on what is being done in the departments and to take corrective action where required. How can the President of the Treasury Board dismiss 14 employees when the workload is going up rather than down? In so doing, he is shirking his responsibilities for fully and effectively applying the Official Languages Act.
Mr. Speaker, the Official Languages Act was adopted, as we know, in July 1988. However, nearly three years later, we are still without regulations on language of work-I stress language of work-and also without regulations on the need to have criteria for equitable participation. So we still lack two parts to go with the Official Languages Act.
Mr. Speaker, I asked the President of the Treasury Board to tell me when we could expect to receive regulations on the language of work from his department. He answered me, and I again quote his answer of March 25:
With respect to the language of work, outside if you will, I believe the official language is already precise enough. As far as I know, there has been no major problem. Should one ever arise, we would be glad to deal with it at the appropriate time and place.
Mr. Speaker, either the President of the Treasury Board does not know what language of work means, which would surprise me, because he is an intelligent man, or his mind was on something other than the House of Commons or he has amnesia. A few days before, in a press release from a public service union, we learned that public servants had difficulty obtaining documentation and the right to communicate with their supervisor in their own language.
By language of work, Mr. Speaker, I mean the ability of public servants to work in either official language. I mean their ability to speak to their supervisor and receive personal services in their own language. I mean their ability to obtain ordinary, everyday material like forms and manuals in the language of their choice. Now,
April 8, 1991

the Commissioner of Official Languages reports on page 135, and I quote:
A large number of supervisors, 25.6 per cent, are still unable to carry out this function in both official languages. As well, there are many others who, having passed a language test and qualified for the bilingualism bonus, make no effort to give their employees freedom of choice in language of work.
So there are no standards, Mr. Speaker. Nearly three years after the passage of the Act, the Commissioner still concludes, on page 132, and I quote:
- that progress towards the language of work objective in federal institutions has stagnated both as a result of the vagueness of current policies and because many senior managers attached no priority to meeting the objective.
And further on, page 136:
It seems clear that the language of work provisions of the 1988 Act will remain a dead letter unless the Governor in Council adopts regulations clarifying the rights of federal employees.
Furthermore, the Professional Institute of the Public Service, a rather well known union, said in a research report that 32.9 per cent of francophones cannot communicate in their language with their supervisor. The Official Languages Commissioner had to report, page 132, that his "words fell on deaf ears" in 1988 and 1989, for his recommendations regarding the establishment of a master plan to ensure implementation of the new Act were not retained.
The President of the Treasury Board answered that question last March 25 when he told me in this House that there was no problem. But there are problems, Mr. Speaker, and the government has to solve them. I feel it is high time for them, the Minister and his government, to remove their blinkers, to realize that regulations are needed. The need is urgent and imperative to ensure respect of both official languages in the workplace. I therefore ask this to the parliamentary secretary: When can we expect regulations about language of work? When can we expect regulations about fair representation?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to reply to the question
Adjournment Debate
posed by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier regarding official language regulations and the regulations on the language of work.
As hon. members are aware, the first priority of this government was to propose regulations on service to the public in English and in French. The President of the Treasury Board tabled such regulations in the House of Commons on November 8, 1990. These proposed regulations have been prepublished in The Canada Gazette, Part I, March 23, 1991.
The Parliamentary Committee on Official Languages is currently studying these proposals. I understand they will shortly be making their recommendations to the President of the Treasury Board.
As the President has already indicated on a number of occasions in this House, these regulatory proposals on serving the public were necessary to complete some key aspects of the Official Languages Act of 1988.
With regard to language of work matters, the Official Languages Act is already quite specific regarding the obligations of federal institutions. The act sets out a number of concrete requirements based on long-standing government policies that remain in place.
Let me just cite a few examples such as the provision of personal and job-related services to employees and work instruments in bilingual districts.
I understand that there were more detailed instructions as required. Treasuiy Board may issue policies or directives according to its mandate under the Official Languages Act.
It is indeed not necessary to regulate all matters. For instance, initiatives to create environments conducive to the effective use of both official languages may be taken without actually issuing regulations. These initiatives could range from federal institutions making special efforts to assist employees returning from language training to use their newly acquired skills in meetings and supervision to develop the bilingual lexicons in special areas. It goes without saying that Treasury Board will continue to carefully examine all matters related to language of work and will strive to ensure that all obligations under the Official Languages Act are met.

April 8, 1991
Adjournment Debate
As for regulations on equitable participation, the Official Languages Act already sets out the government's long standing commitment in this area. I can tell hon. members that we are committed to ensure that English speaking and French speaking Canadians have equal opportunities to obtain employment and advancement in federal institutions. Current government policies are clear and explicit on this matter. In fact, participation levels in the Public Service broadly reflect those found in the appropriate sectors of the national labour force.
Any specific imbalances, such as anglophone participation in federal institutions in Quebec for example, are being dealt with by Treasury Board and the institutions concerned. Issuing regulations on language of work and equitable participation do not appear to be necessary at this time.
Moreover, I can assure hon. members that this government will continue to actively meet its obligations and commitments to the Canadian public and to its employees in accordance with the Official Languages Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, do you remember the green plan? Do you remember the government's promise of significant and real progress in tackling environmental problems? The minister and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources seem to have forgotten. At least that is the message in the latest budget.
For the seventh year in a row the department's funding of energy efficiency, conservation and alternatives was cut. Last year's already pathetic $40 million was cut another 12 per cent down to $35 million. That is a whopping cut of $375 million, 91 per cent in this budget item since 1984 when the budget was $410 million, the first year of the Conservative government's reign.
By contrast, in 1991-92 the government will be spending $154.8 million as a loan for the Husky Oil upgrader at Lloydminster and $180.6 million in the Hibernia project. That is more than $335 million in two oil megaprojects in 1991-92 alone. That is almost 10 times the entire budget for all energy efficiency, conservation and alternatives.
In the case of Hibernia, the government will be giving over $1 billion of taxpayers' money-that's right, a $1 billion gift-to a consortium that is planning to ship virtually all Hibernia oil straight to the United States. It will not even be refined in Canada. That $1 billion give to Hibernia, a straight subsidy to American consumers, would have paid for this government's measly annual funding commitment to all energy efficiency, conservation and alternatives-remember, Mr. Speaker, $35 million-for over 28 years.
Again, by contrast, this year the government will funnel $215 million into nuclear power development through Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. and the Atomic Energy Control Board and there is more. According to a speech the minister gave June 5, 1990, to the Canadian Nuclear Association, Canada has invested a staggering $30 billion in nuclear facilities. Presumably this includes the $40 million per year that AECL spent over the last 10 years just to investigate sweeping its radioactive waste into a hole in the Canadian Shield.
One final contrast, even after just six months in power the New Democratic Government of Ontario has already left the Mulroney Conservatives far behind on environmentally responsible energy policy. As just one example, the Ontario government has ordered Ontario Hydro to divert $240 million-that is $60 million a year for four years-from nuclear energy development into reducing electricity demand through energy conservation and efficiency.
That diversion alone is worth more than one and a half times the total annual energy department spending on all federal programs for efficiency, conservation and alternate energy. Indeed that total federal budget of $35 million is only a little over twice what Ontario Hydro will spend each year merely on advertising its conservation and efficiency programs.
I should point out as well that Ontario Hydro is subsidizing the federal government in a pilot project to save energy in about 60 federal government buildings. That project, to install new lighting, motors and insulation, which reportedly will save the federal government $860,000 a year in energy costs, is being extended to all federal buildings in Ontario. I do hope that this program will demonstrate to the Mulroney Conservatives just what a little leadership can do.
April 8, 1991

Less than two weeks ago, on March 25, the all party House of Commons Standing Committee on the Environment tabled its report on global warming. This unanimous report entitled Out of Balance-the Risks of Irreversible Climate Change warns that the phenomenon of global warming is a fact and it poses a severe threat to Canada and to the planet as a whole.
The report obviously supports what the minister stated in a speech he gave in Toronto on September 13, 1989, and I quote:
The greatest reductions in carbon dioxide can be obtained through energy efficiency and conservation.
Having made these remarks, the minister then cut the budget for energy efficiency and conservation by a two-year total of 28 per cent.
The minister still talks a good line. He was quoted in a Globe and Mail article of March 30, 1991 apparently qualifying remarks-laughable in a morbid sort of way when you consider this government's massive bias against energy efficiency and alternatives in favour of fossil fuel and nuclear megaprojects-that the Mulroney Conservatives have a "market based" approach to energy policy. Said Mr. Epp:
I think it is the role of an energy minister to get us into areas where the present infrastructure will not take us. If people argue that I am moving away from the marketplace, I will accept that charge.
Mr. Speaker, I pray for the day when I will be able honestly to level that charge.
Perhaps, just maybe, the minister is beginning to believe some of the good advice he has been receiving. For example, in March 1989, his department received a report entitled Energy Demand in Canada, 1973-1987, which included a series of proposals for future policies and programs. It says, and I quote:
To achieve the major economic and environmental benefits that energy efficiency still has to offer, government policies and programs for the future will need to emphasize a strategic combination of, energy efficient standards; improved information programs; financial incentives, and Research Development and Demonstration assistance.
To rely solely on energy prices and existing market mechanisms is a formula for failure. Active and constructive intervention in the marketplace is absolutely essential.
In Halifax last June 18, just 11 days after his bill to authorize the bill dollar gift to Hibernia passed second
Adjournment Debate
reading, the minister told members of the Solar Energy Society of Canada that, and again I quote:
It is clear that a safe, environmentally sound and economically viable energy path is imperative for this country. For this reason, we are firmly committed to the expansion of the efficiency and alternative energy sector. Like you, we want it to play a much larger role in Canada's energy economy.
The words and the evidence are clearly at odds. So my question to the parliamentary secretary is this. In view of this government's repeated funding cuts to energy conservation, efficiency and alternatives, what conclusion can Canadians draw other than that this government's actions, contrasted with its claim to be truly committed to energy conservation, efficiency and alternatives, merely demonstrates its stunning hypocrisy?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada is committed to the goal of maintaining and enhancing the environmental quality and in the green plan as set out by a comprehensive framework for the achievement of this goal.
The green plan contains strategies for improving the quality of air, land and water. The green plan promises that as a part of the strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, the government will take several specific actions. It will implement the National Action Strategy on global warming that will be a comprehensive approach, cast in the international context, emphasize flexibility to take account of new information and developments and recognize regional differences.
It will table a National Energy Efficiency Alternative Energy Act dealing with the regulation of energy efficiency levels in energy-using equipment, labelling of products to convey information on energy use, and collection of statistics on energy use.
It will set minimum energy efficiency standards for appliances and equipment.
It will improve and expand the present Energuide program for energy labelling of home appliances.
It will update and regionalize the federal Measures for Energy Conservation in new buildings, and encourage their incorporation in building codes.
It will improve the energy efficiency of transportation by setting new fuel efficiency standards, helping to inform fleet managers and drivers and working with the

April 8, 1991
Adjournment Debate
provinces and municipalities on improvements in the transportation system.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will establish a National Advisory Council to promote government industry co-operation and to establish energy efficiency targets for each of Canada's industrial sectors. Alternative energy sources will be encouraged through accelerated development of market penetration of alternative transportation fuels, including expansion of natural gas markets, increased availability of alternative fuel vehicles and support for research and development.
This hon. member is incorrect in his statement that EMR has reduced funding for efficiency and alternative energy in the fiscal year 1991-92. The government's estimates tabled recently projected expenditures of $34.7 million, slightly higher than the level of expenditures for the fiscal year 1990-91.
While the hon. member chooses to criticize the government for its current spending levels on efficiency and alternative energy programs, he does so most selectively. What he fails to acknowledge is that for all intents and purposes, spending reductions on these programs were due to the government's commitment to erase the last vestiges of the National Energy Program. Moreover, spending on efficiency and alternative energy under the NEP provided for a cumbersome and ineffective manner.
Four years and millions of dollars later, taxpayers were shown little return on their investment.
This government and our department is committed to the green plan and committed, Sir, to ensure that all Canadians have an equal opportunity to work and also being able to ensure that we have an environment for the future.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to speak on a subject of the utmost importance for the people of the Montreal area. I am referring to the disastrous job situation and economic conditions in Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time I raise this question. I raised it over six times since February 25 and I have not yet received a satisfactory answer.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that this government has forgotten Montreal. On December 10,
1990.1	asked a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration regarding the deplorable job situation in the province of Quebec. At that time, 87,000 jobs had been lost in Quebec just over a six month period.
The minister told me, at the time, that employment programs were available in Quebec and that I would be happy with the results they would produce.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I am still not satisfied with the efforts made by this government to create jobs in the Montreal area. That is why I raised the question again on March 18. So, Mr. Speaker, let us look at what results the employment initiatives of this government have produced.
In Montreal, today, one person out of four is living below the threshold of poverty. The unemployment rate for the region encompassing the Montreal area reached
15.1	per cent in February according to Statistics Canada.
These are the results of the employment policies of this government and the reason why I raise the subject again tonight.
Economic conditions in Montreal are so bad that the unemployment rate is higher there than in any other city in Canada. The situation is getting worse and we have no economic recovery programs in place.
Based on the report the SECOR counsulting group presented to the Quebec government, an estimated
615,000	people are living in poverty in the Montreal area. Nowadays, that is unacceptable!
On March 18, the Minister of Labour told me that his government had invested millions of dollars over the past two years to help stimulate the economy in Montreal.
Where has that money gone? The economic situation in Montreal only got worse. In the La Presse issue of March 28, we can read that 60 per cent of the welfare recipients in Montreal have been on welfare rolls for more than two years.
We must conclude, that this government's action does not improve in any way Montrealers' standard of living. Indeed, one would be wrong to say that because the
April 8, 1991

initiatives of this government have had one result: to throw Canada's economy and Montreal's in particular into a slump. They have destroyed families by depriving them of their income, of their jobs and of their salaries.
On March 18, the minister of Labour has stressed that in order to create jobs it was necessary to teach people new technologies. But, I told him that a new knowledge is useless if one is unable to put it into practice. A person will be able to put his newly acquired knowledge to good use only if we create new jobs and if Canadians have a renewed faith in their economy. Unfortunately, this government has managed to achieve exactly the opposite, since jobs are more difficult to find and Canadians in general have less confidence in the economy.
So, Mr. Speaker, when we look at the situation today, we see that in Quebec the bankruptcy rate has increased by 40 per cent in the first few months in 1991. According to Statistics Canada, 1,618 individuals have asked for the protection of the Bankruptcy Act. If the minister wants to increase confidence in the economy, these figures won't help. As for the government's effort to create jobs, I would say their record leaves much to be desired.
I have just mentioned to the minister that people need jobs in which they can use their new knowledge. However, by reducing funds for research and development, the government is not encouraging job creation. Between 1987 and 1990, government spending in that area decreased from 1.4 per cent to 1.28 per cent of the GNP. Mr. Speaker, again, I ask the government: How will they resolve the unemployment problem in greater Montreal and throughout the vast Montreal region? What will they do to help save the 1,800 jobs being threatened at General Motors, in Boisbriand, in the Sainte-Therese area? What measures will they introduce to put Montreal's economy back on track? What help will they provide to the 225,000 unemployed in the Montreal region to finally revitalize this economy the government seems to have forgotten?
Mr. Speaker, I know my time is almost up. I just wanted to explain how it feels to read articles such as there: Poverty gaining ground in the Montreal region;
615,000	people living in poor households, 50 per cent in Montreal. Montreal, once the biggest city in Canada, has
Adjournment Debate
become the unemployment capital of Canada, the welfare capital of our country. The time has come for this government to assume its responsibilities and stop the dramatic loss of our country's very valuable human resources.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Employment and Immigration, I wish to respond in greater detail to the questions of March 13 by the member for Saint-Leonard.
Let me first say something about jobs. Between 1980 and 1984 when the Liberal government was in power,
4,000	jobs were lost in Montreal. Between March 1985 and March 1991, 96,000 net jobs were created in Montreal. We know that more needs to be done, but the hon. member belittles that great city if he paints a picture of unrelieved gloom.
We know assistance is necessary. The statistics make that clear. This government is taking a number of measures beneficial to the economy of Quebec, and Montreal in particular. Agreement has been signed with the province of Quebec to spend $440 million in federal funding over five years, between 1988 and 1993, on economic development in all regions of Quebec.
The government is very concerned about the challenges faced by certain neighbourhoods in Montreal, especially the southwest. In April 1989 the federal government responded to the Creesom report and announced that it would provide the following assistance in southwest Montreal:
Employment and Immigration Canada will allocate $32.5 million over the next five years on various labour market initiatives. The government intends to work with the local community to develop sustainable jobs and more qualified labour. For the last two years it has been working with RESO, an economic development corporation, to establish training priorities. For example, EIC is presently developing with RESO a special school where local residents can receive training assistance.
Industry, science and technology will provide $15 million to establish an industrial recovery program for southwest Montreal.
The federal government will also provide housing and financial assistance to southwest Montreal. Forty-eight million dollars in Federal Business Development Bank loans has been allocated over the next five years to promote economic activity in this area.

April 8, 1991
Adjournment Debate
There are many more assistance projects that have been announced by this government:
In November 1990 the Department of Employment and Immigration allocated $2 million to establish in east Montreal a petrochemical training centre. This will respond to that industry's need for skilled workers.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy also helps. In 1990-91, $32 million in Canadian Jobs Strategy funding has enabled 7,925 Montrealers to participate in training programs. Furthermore, a total of 46 industrial adjustment committees are active in the Montreal region.
Finally, I understand the member's concern with the Montreal economy and the job market. This government was concerned with this particular issue long before the members opposite chose to focus on the unemployment statistics.
For example, the government fought for Bill C-22, the pharmaceuticals bill, which brought investment and jobs to this city. The members opposite did not want this legislation and delayed it for 17 months.
The government knew that a more innovative approach to labour market programs was needed in early
1989, and yet Bill C-21 came into force only in late 1990. Had we had Bill C-21 in place in January 1990, $800 million in UI training expenditures would have been spent last year in this country. Montreal would have benefited, but had to wait until the opposition made up its mind.
In conclusion, the government is helping the Montreal petrochemical industry, an industry which was all but completely abandoned by the former government.
This government is helping the Montreal and Quebec economy, and it did so long before the opposition woke up in March and chose to focus its attention for the first time on the state of the Montreal economy.
