speakeroldname: Hon. John A. Fraser (Speaker of the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The right hon. Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. President, Madam Salinas, Mr. Speaker, cher collegues, mesdames et messieurs'.
During my visit to Mexico last year, Mr. President, we laid the foundation of a new beginning in relations between Mexico and Canada. Today with your visit here all of us build on that foundation, and on behalf of the people of Canada I extend to you, Mr. President, to Mrs. Salinas, your family, and all members of the Mexican delegation the warmest of welcomes to our country, Canada.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Formal diplomatic relations between Canada and Mexico go back many decades. First contacts date to the days of Captain George Vancouver who gave Canada's largest Pacific island its original name, "Vancouver Y Quadra", after himself and the commander of the Spanish vessels, Mexicana and Sutil with whom he sailed.

If Canada and Mexico grew on the same continent, each tended to look elsewhere, however, for like-minded partners. But the world around us is changing dramatically and economic competition and opportunity are the hallmarks of our age. And so it is no coincidence that both of us have re-calibrated our global orientations and re-formulated our foreign policy priorities, at about the same time.
Since you came to office, Mexico has been focusing more northward to the United States, our common neighbour, and to Canada, to build new partnerships to improve the lives of your people. And Canada has begun to focus more southward, to consolidate our base in the hemisphere and to pursue new opportunities in the global economy.
Our first step in implementing this new policy direction was to conclude a free trade relationship with the United States. As you know, the decision to secure that free trade relationship was supported 100 per cent by all Canadians and all members of this House of Commons.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Well, give or take a few.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
The next step was to develop a comprehensive strategy for relations with Latin America. By the year 2000, 600 million people with a purchasing power of $1 trillion will live in Latin America. It will constitute a continent of enormous economic power and great political influence on the world stage.
As part of our strategy for relations with Latin America we have joined the Organization of American States, both to demonstrate our commitment to progress in this hemisphere and also to play our part in making it happen. A lynch pin of our strategy is our renewed relationship with Mexico.
April 8, 1991

During my visit to Mexico last year we concluded 10 agreements covering a wide range of public policy issues from law enforcement to environmental protection. Today, four more agreements are being signed; on film co-production, double taxation, and on commerce, including a $500 million line of credit between EDC and Pemex.
These agreements are further building blocks in the construction of our new relationship.
A North American free trade agreement is a logical next step. That is why, Mr. President, we have endorsed your proposal for such an agreement. We know that the road will be long and difficult. We know it is a courageous decision by you, Mr. President, and all parliamentarians wish you well.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
A North American free trade agreement would create a market of over 350 million people with a gross product of over $7 trillion, bigger than the European Community whose economic relationships will intensify greatly in 1992.

Trade in goods and service would exceed $300 billion per year. Canadian consumers would benefit from the lower prices that competition and comparative advantage can deliver. And Canadian producers would benefit competitively from the restructuring and modernization that access to a larger market makes possible.
We have no intention, however, of renegotiating the Canada-U.S.A., FTA. We want to build on the FTA and to expand trade liberalization to encompass all of North America.
The objective of all three governments is to negotiate an agreement that allows them to strengthen their economies through free trade, for the benefit of their people.

The advantages for Mexico are clear. If there is one lesson that globalization and interdependence have taught, it is that increased trade brings higher living standards and greater opportunities. Trade, not aid, has opened up the most effective avenues to prosperity and to social justice. Aid, while extremely helpful has not itself been able to deliver prosperity. But trade, by transforming developing nations into advanced economies, has done so.
Not so long ago Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan were considered to be underdeveloped centres of low-cost labour. But as a result of sound economic policies at home and increased trade abroad, the standard of living in these countries on a per capita basis, is on a track to parity with the western industrialized countries during this decade. This is an extraordinary achievement and I think it is one that Mexico is going to emulate.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Countries with strong economies can afford to provide their citizens with social benefits that others cannot. These same countries are also those that can afford to impose the most stringent environmental standards on their industries and on their citizens. They are also the countries that dominate international trade.
Mr. President, 87 per cent of Canadian imports now come from the United States, Europe and Japan, and not from, for example, countries with extremely low wage rates such as China or India or the Soviet Union. The argument that wage structures in less developed nations somehow fundamentally distort a free trade area, or provide substantially unfair advantages, does not stand up to serious scrutiny.
The reality is that in the knowledge age we live in, competitiveness depends not on one, but on many factors, including education, training, productivity, communications and transportation networks, proximity to markets, and the costs of capital as well as the costs of labour.

The Government of Canada believes that a Canada-U.S.-Mexico free trade agreement can prove to be in the best interests of all concerned-if it can be achieved on terms that are acceptable to all three sovereign nations.
But important as the trade issue is, there is much more on the agenda of our two countries. Cooperation is underway on environmental protection. Business links are growing between private enterprise on both sides. And 350,000 Canadian tourists and business people visited Mexico last year.

April 8, 1991
Talks between President Salinas and I will address the evolving situation in this hemisphere to which he, as President of Mexico, brings a unique perspective. And our talks will go beyond respective domestic and regional concerns to the ongoing challenges in the Persian Gulf, the evolving situation in the Soviet Union, the prospects for successful conclusion of multilateral trade negotiations and the urgent need to limit the spread of weapons of mass destruction and to control the sale of arms.

Mr. Speaker, simply put, there would be no discussion today of a resurgent Mexico, much less of a North American free trade agreement, were it not for President Salinas. His confidence in Mexicans and their confidence in themselves, have made it possible to transform attitudes, to accomplish changes and to chart a course that even five years ago seemed unthinkable.
Canadians respect Mexico's dynamism, and all Canadians admire Mexico's culture. We welcome you today, Mr. President, as the visionary leader of a great people with an exciting future. Here in the House of Commons, this crucible of Canadian democracy, I invite you now, on behalf of all parliamentarians of all political parties, who value our association with Mexico-and all of us do-I invite you today to address the Parliament and the people of Canada.

Hear, hear.
His Excellency Carlos Salinas de Gortari (President of Mexico):
[His Excellency spoke in Spanish.]

The Hon. John A. Fraser, Speaker of the House of Commons of Canada; the Hon. Guy Charbonneau, Speaker of the Senate of Canada; the Right Hon. Brian Mulroney, Prime Minister of Canada; hon. members of the House of Commons and Senate of Canada; Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen: I come here in respectful response to the invitation extended to me by this sovereign body, which so worthily represents the people of Canada. In this house of democracy resides the will of the great Canadian nation to find its own answers
to its needs and to forge its own path in the world. I bring to this rostrum the friendship of the Mexican people and speak with their voice in expressing our desire for Mexico and Canada to become better acquainted with their many coinciding aspects, as well as with the wealth of their differences, so that together we may embark on new relations of exchanges and co-operation for our mutual benefit.
Canada and Mexico are both the outcome of singular experiences, but both are genuine nations, soundly rooted in their history and solidly backing their national project. Here in this Parliament speaks the voice of a sensitive and vigorous country that jealously guards its linguistic and cultural traditions and cherishes peace and co-operation among nations. Mexico draws its identity from a synthesis of civilizations and cultures; the strength of our blending of races gradually built up a national character that is proud of its past, aware that it is the heir and custodian not only of universal values but also of its own way of life and profound communal solidarity.
Mexico has a robust identity and sufficient vitality to build its own sovereign future. We therefore do not fear an encounter with the world, rather we actively seek it. To be bent on autarky would not only be Utopian, but would mean condemning ourselves to backwardness and marginalization. Our homeland is able to look out at the world and open itself up to contact with other peoples, without thereby failing to be faithful to itself, to its traditions and culture, to its values and historical raison d'etre. We Mexicans today look towards the future and are determined to play a significant role in the coming century.
That is why I have come to Canada, an industrialized nation with a high export volume, a wealth of natural resources and a wide rate of freedoms, which will undoubtedly contribute to shaping the world of the third millennium. The Mexican people want to establish new continental relations that are more dynamic, more productive and more just. By doing so, our governments will be in a better position to carry out their tasks in a manner befitting the men and women of our countries and our times, who are doing their best to make our hemisphere an area of convergence and freedoms. We can take advantage of the goodwill and hard work of our peoples to guide our agreements and encounters to our mutual
April 8, 1991

benefit and ensure that this new world will once again astonish humanity, just as it did 500 years ago.
Members of Parliament: Today, as we are just beginning to witness the end of the world's post-war structure, we recognize the crafty barriers and outworn dogmas that are designed to hinder the exchange of ideas, goods and people. The new co-operation between the great powers, the autumn revolution in central and eastern Europe, the new democracies here in the Americas, evinced, to our fascination, the global nature of the human condition, the flexibility of politics and the economic interdependence of nations. The Persian Gulf conflict was a painful reminder of the same global reality. Today, it is no longer possible to dream of an isolated social experience, impenetrable to coexistence or to alien conflicts. The hope and the challenge of building a world governed by international law are growing at a parallel rate. The true challenge of our times is to recognize the constructive force of the globalization of history, to face with responsibility and respect the variety of social experience and to avert the risk of new attempts at protagonism and new myths aimed at ignoring the sovereignty rights of states.
The world economy is the stage of a harsh and intense competition for markets. The revolution in knowledge and technology is transforming work habits and making social relations more fluid. New centres of innovation, resources and trade are at the forefront of economic activity and are forming into blocs to profit from then-comparative advantages. To have staying power in this new international arena demands changes in economic structures, openness to competition and innovation, and new forms of association both within and outside the borders of individual nations.
In view of those circumstances, Mexico has set out to make the changes needed to secure a new placement in the world economy and to play an active role in the political configuration of the future. Within our borders, Mexican society has undergone a significant transformation over the past 25 years. Our current population of 82 million will increase by a further 10 million during my administration. Every year, one million young people seek to join administration. Every year, one million young people seek to join the labour force. Then-demands are clear-cut. They want opportunities, services, and to participate in the decisions that concern
them as well as in national affairs. They now reflect the demands of a better-informed and therefore politically more active, mature society. That is why in Mexico development, democracy and, above all, solidarity with those who have the least are essential needs and not merely options for defining government policies. Our response has had to be commensurate with these legitimate demands and in keeping with the new global reality.
We have strengthened our democratic institutions by changing the customs and practices that hampered the indispensable modernization of our structures. Thus, we now have a more vigorous system of parties in which increased electoral competition is the distinctive characteristic of political contention. The progress of democracy in Mexico has been reflected in the establishment of a new juridical framework for electoral matters, the result of an agreement reached between the different and even opposing political forces in the country. This new electoral legislation ensures a framework agreed upon with a view to establishing mutual responsibilities and acceptance of electoral results. We Mexicans know that our greatest political challenge lies in renovating our democratic practices, organization and structures in unison, so as to respond to an increasingly demanding society.
Mexico has never lost its course on the road to democracy. However, if politics are to be constructive, favourable economic conditions need to be established- as many fledgling democracies are beginning to discover-to ensure that the aspirations and ideals of liberty are solidly founded in actual reality in order to be long-lasting. The democratic exercise of power therefore also involved building economic foundations that will give our people more and better opportunities to realize their hopes for a decent life.
In Mexico, it is through our modernization strategy that we have sought to regain the path to gradual, sustained growth. After two years of persevering joint efforts in that direction made by society and the government, we have succeeded in achieving a growth rate of 4 per cent of GNP in real terms, and in reducing the public deficit to just half a percentage point of our national product, the lowest level in a quarter of a century. Strict fiscal discipline and a successful, timely renegotiation of the foreign debt have provided the necessary stability. Moreover, the pact signed by all sectors of society to

April 8, 1991
reduce inflation remains in force, and this year we aim to cut it back to half the rate recorded in 1990.
During the past two years, Mexicans have seen inflation reduced more than it had been over the past 20 years. Our objective is to lower it to single-digit levels comparable to those of our main trading partners and to provide the greatest possible certainty regarding the development of our economy.
Economic stability has therefore been our highest priority. From the outset we viewed it as an essential condition for ensuring the continuity and viability of the structural measures that we have implemented in order to modernize our productive plant. The main objective is to make Mexico a major exporting country: hence the urgent need to ensure greater efficiency in productive processes and over-all quality of the end product. That is why we opened up our economy to international and domestic competition. In a brief period of time, we moved from being one of the most closed developing economies to being one of the most open. We have dismantled non-tariff barriers, removing them from over 85 per cent of imports; tariffs now average 10 per cent and the highest stands at 20 per cent. We needed to encourage innovation and competition, and to take advantage of the arbitrage of foreign prices on domestic prices.
That, in turn, meant broadening and stepping up the process of deregulating large sectors of our economy and establishing more attractive conditions to encourage greater flows of foreign direct investment, on which access to new technology largely depends. The fields of transportation, telecommunications and secondary petrochemicals are now more efficient and competitive; new regulations afford security and certainty to foreign investors who now have 100 per cent access to investment in activities that account for nearly two-thirds of our GNP. The Mexican Congress is currently studying bills to define clear, competitive rules for the protection of intellectual property rights. The climate for investment is attractive and dependable. This year Mexico has witnessed the arrival of nearly $4 billion in foreign investment and we expect more in the future.
Another important structural change has lain in the sale of public companies that are not of a strategic or priority nature. Our State has grown not only in terms of bureaucracy but also of property. The economic crisis of the past decade revealed the seriousness of the problem. More state-owned property and greater trade protectionism in Mexico simply did not lead to greater justice or greater economic strength that would allow us to deal with international contingencies and grow. The government has therefore privatized mining industries and companies, our airlines, and the telephone company, and soon to come are the commercial banks. The funds obtained from such sales have aided financial stability and have been invested in tackling extreme poverty. The Mexican people realize that government responsibility does not lie in owning a new fleet of aeroplanes or new bank offices, but in meeting demands for water and schools, and in providing opportunities for Indian, rural and urban communities. That is why Mexicans support the government's programs for change and thereby guarantee the continuity of such programs.
This shows the magnitude of the efforts made by the Mexican people. The strength of the nation and its increased capability to meet domestic needs and the demands resulting from globalization of the economy rest on a firm foundation. Consequently, we now intend to step up the process of diversifying our ties and bolstering trade relations with the various regional integration areas. We are aware of the potential of our geographic location, which makes us, like Canada, neighbours of the world's strongest economy and a link between the Orient and the Occident. We are also aware that Mexico is a bridge connecting the northern and southern parts of the hemisphere, which implies greater two-way trade with the countries of Latin America and therefore a secure link in shaping a continent-wide, free trade area.
Consequently, we have begun talks with Canada and the United States of America that will, in the near future, enable us to embark on negotiations leading to the signing of a trilateral free trade treaty. I am convinced that such a treaty is unquestionably the best option for the parties involved. It is an opportunity for our three nations to create a major economic zone that while respecting our cultural differences, will have the
April 8, 1991

vitality to compete successfully with the European market and the Asian Pacific Rim.
Within the framework of an agreement between sovereign nations that will do away with tariff and non-tariff barriers, increase the expand trade patterns and objectively and justly resolve differences, we can expect investment and the creation of jobs to benefit all three countries. We will also be able to find economies of scale that will not only increase the competitiveness of Canada and restore that of the United States, but also bring Mexico's competitiveness up to world levels. A new array of technological options may well open up as a result of greater specialization and diversification in production and exports. We have what is needed to translate efforts into well-being for the inhabitants of North America.
Particularly for a country such as Canada, where the export of goods and services accounts for one-fourth of the gross domestic product, Mexico's market, in full expansion with 82 million consumers, is a potential destination for Canadian products and investment. Correspondingly, Mexico is seeking free and reciprocal access for its products to Canada and the United States. Furthermore, we are convinced that such conditions will generate greater investment and more sources of well-paid jobs, which will dissuade our fellow countrymen from leaving Mexico in search of job opportunities in the north. Economic relations with the United States are already strong, but we now wish to ensure that they grow in an organized and equitable manner, taking into account differences in the levels of development achieved by the two economies.
Very broad opportunities truly exist, since the economies of Canada and Mexico are complementary. Mexico is seeking to gain from Canadian experience in the fields where Canada has consolidated advanced infrastructure and has leading-edge technology. Such fields include, for example, telecommunications and public transportation, advanced irrigation projects, and water and environmental sanitation. Efforts to modernize Mexico urgently call for access to different technological options that will give producers greater flexibility in meeting the expectations of modem consumers.
Freer trade between our nations is expected to enhance the well-being of our peoples. We must not blame free trade for the conditions imposed on the productive
situation by other factors. We have nothing to fear but barriers and obstacles that are intended to protect some parties from competition and, in doing so, end up destroying creativity and well-being. We must not forget that, sooner or later, such barriers have been demolished by the freedom-seeking vitality of peoples and by then-demands for justice.
Distinguished members of Parliament, a free trade agreement between Canada and the United States of America is already in force. Arduous and intense negotiations preceded the signing of this agreement and now serve as valuable experience of which Mexico hopes to take advantage. Although the debate was undoubtedly intense, it was finally shown that the economic prosperity of Canada, one of the world's most important exporting countries, is closely linked to access to new markets and consequently to plans for developing a free trade in goods and services. An economy that closes itself off loses competitiveness. An economy that is skilfully opened up gains new competitive vitality.
In Mexico we share this vocation. It is with the support of our culture and our history that we are opening up to the world and to the competition for markets. We know that the path that each nation pursues cannot be other than the result of its own historic experience, of the specific circumstances of its geography and even of the resources with which nature has endowed it. In the world of today, however, comparative advantages are not inflexible-they can be built up. The circumstances of today's world oblige us to make use of all the energy, imagination and determination of Canadians and Mexicans alike in working toward the convergence of our goals, so as to take full advantage of the complementary aspects of our economies. We can share a vision of the future, based on the long term, that will heed the needs of coming generations, who deserve to live in a better world.
We have embarked upon a new and vigorous stage in bilateral relations between Canada and Mexico. We are counting upon the spirit of our societies and the interest of our governments to strengthen our ties in the different areas of our agenda, both as regards our economies and in the fields of politics and culture. In particular, we in Mexico want to intensify the co-operation between our countries in two areas that the Mexican government and people regard as especially sensitive. These are: the

April 8, 1991
fight to definitively eradicate the scourge of drug trafficking, and the mutually respectful and concerted effort to improve the environment.
The international struggle against illegal traffic in narcotics is Mexico's struggle as well. Over the past two years, we have seized thousands of tons of cocaine and destroyed hundreds of hectares of marijuana and poppies; we have broken up over 100 criminal organizations and confiscated their goods and properties; we have substantially increased budgetary resources for combating drugs and raised penalties and sanctions against those proven to have a connection to this chain of terror; we have ratified the Vienna Convention and are playing an active role in international forums. We have carried out these and other actions because in Mexico we consider drug trafficking to be a basic threat to the security of our country and to the health of our young people. We know that this chain of criminal activity transcends the frontiers of any country-which means that co-operation among nations is essential. Nonetheless, for it to be truly effective, such co-operation must be respectful of the sovereignty of all the states involved.
In the protection of the environment, Mexico assumes its commitment along with the entire world, because it sees this as a humanitarian cause of universal scope. Mexico has gladly accepted its responsibility in this crusade that is incumbent upon us all, since all of us stand to benefit from its advances and its successes. We Mexicans are convinced that our growth need not lead to the ravaging and pollution of the environment; quite the contrary. Growth that damages the environment is not growth. Resources and technologies for cleaning it up are still needed, but with government and society working together we have made progress.
A few days ago the Mexican Government took the decision to definitively close down one of our country's five refineries, precisely the one that supplied Mexico City. This was done at great economic cost, but this action will prevent the release of 80 thousand tons of pollutants per year into the atmosphere. We are also going to make other heavy investments in improving the environment of Mexico City, but we realize that a great deal still remains to be done, not only in our capital city but also in other areas of our country, some of which
have been declared part of the patrimony of humanity. The initial and long-term efforts must be made by the Mexicans themselves, but we also propose to obtain more far-reaching international co-operation in this endeavour. I must acknowledge that our efforts have been supported by the invaluable technological and financial assistance of friendly countries, among them Canada, for which I hereby extend the sincere and fraternal gratitude of the people of Mexico.
Honourable Members of Parliament, Mexico has always based its foreign policy on strict observance of the principles that define harmonious coexistence among nations. By tradition and conviction, Mexico has displayed a clear vocation for peace and conduct consistent with respect for the self-determination of peoples, the peaceful settlement of controversies and co-operation for development. For that reason, and because of the strength of its history, Mexico has confidence in its future, in the deep-seated nationalism of its people, and in the vigour of an ancient culture, which is experiencing a renewal and renaissance, and which proudly offers to the world's surprised eyes the contributions stemming from the spirit of its men and its women to the vast cultural wealth of the west.
Today Mexico, proud of its past, looks to the future. In doing so, we have found in Canada a friendly and respectful nation, interested in becoming acquainted with our way of life. We Mexicans also want to gain a better knowledge of this country's way of life, to explore in depth the traditions and customs of the people of Canada, and to enrich ourselves with the value that they themselves place on their pluralistic society and the diversity of their ethnic groups and their languages.
In the spirit of a Canadian who so staunchly demonstrated the strength of his determination, Terry Fox, as in the impressive talent of men of science like Frederick Banting and the humanism of Stephen Leacock, we Mexicans have come to know of the greatness of your people. That is why we are certain that this new era of friendship can be positive and enduring. The people of Mexico make very good friends. They want to be, in the true sense of the word, friends of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Guy Charbonneau (Speaker of the Senate):
speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Your Excellency, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Prime Minister, honor-ables collegues du Senat et de la Chambre des Communes, distinguished guests:
April 8, 1991

[Editor's Note: Speaker spoke in Spanish.]

Mr. President, we are honoured by your visit. Your stature as an economist and a humanist inspires us with trust borne of reason. The validity of your democratic convictions is testimony of mutually beneficial co-operation.

You embody our countries' hope to create organic ties on this North American continent which we share with a powerful neighbour.
A worthy representative of contemporary Mexico, in your writings and your political life, you have already shown that technology and human values are not opposed but, on the contrary, that they combine to enrich humanity.

It is entirely appropriate, Your Excellency, that you should visit our assembly at this historic juncture in Canadian-Mexican relations. Mexico is of immense importance to Canada.
Before today, - we knew you as a forward-looking leader determined to reshape your nation to meet the challenges of the future, while preserving the diversity of your cultural traditions and a deep sense of national pride in the achievements of previous civilizations.
Today, we have had the privilege of hearing you speak eloquently of your vision of the Mexico of today and tomorrow, and we feel that under your leadership the aspirations of your people are in good hands.
Your bold vision for the future of North America opens the door to new avenues of co-operation which promise to carry us well into the next century. Time strengthens friendship, and we look forward to expanding our ties in the months and years ahead.
In listening to you, Mr. President, we realized once again how the firmness of your ideological convictions is yet allied to a wise pragmatism, and your courage to a political wisdom which commands respect.
Mr. President, your mother is an economist and your father a senator; your inheritance was obviously the presidency.
We are proud to share our coming prospects with a neighbour who so profoundly grasps the interdependence of the modem world.
Your country is indebted to you for a new deal for its people. Your knowledge and experience fit you perfectly to play a prime role in the new deal that the three neighbouring countries in North America are contemplating. And we have the greatest confidence in the man who started the process, the President of Mexico, whom we have the honour to welcome here today.
On behalf of my colleagues in the Senate of Canada, your Excellency, allow me to thank you very warmly for your inspiring address to us today and for your moving expressions of friendship for the Canadian people.
We would ask you to carry back to Mexico a message of the deep friendship which all Canadians feel for the Mexican people.

I thank you, Mr. President, and wish you good luck.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Your Excellency, Madam, Mr. Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker of the Senate, Members of the House of Commons and Senate, honoured and distin-gued guests, ladies and gentlemen:
Today, I have the duty but also the immense pleasure to express on behalf of all members of the House of Commons and of all political parties represented here our great joy in having you among us in this historic Chamber.
Canada and Mexico have enjoyed an enduring friendship over many years. Since diplomatic relations were established in 1942, we have maintained positive and constructive contacts for our mutual benefit in numerous spheres of activity.
I should mention, Mr. President, the continual exchanges that have taken place between members of your Parliament and members of our Parliament over many years which have had a great effect in understanding both among your own people and among our colleagues that you meet with today.
I might say from a personal point of view that before I was elected to this House, I visited your country as part of a bidding delegation for the 1976 Winter Olympics,

April 8, 1991
when you were holding the Olympics in 1968. We were very well received by your representatives and they got us the Olympics. They got us the Summer Olympics though, not the Winter Olympics.
I have also had the privilege of being on a parliamentary delegation visiting your country. I want you to take back to your colleagues the very great importance that we place on these exchanges.
Today, we are facing new challenges arising from vast changes in our hemisphere and the world community, and you have spoken of them. In your address to us today, you have not ignored the difficult questions but rather with statements of courage and vision you have drawn attention to them.
As a true leader, you have reminded us that a challenge is also an opportunity. Since assuming office you have achieved great progress in moving Mexican society forward to realize its true potential.
Those of us who have had the opportunity to visit your country are impressed with the vast storehouse of resources, both material and human, with which your country is blessed. Culturally rich, economically dynamic, historically resplendent, politically self-assured, Mexico cannot help but succeed. These values and attitudes are reflected in the views you have expressed to us today.
The comments that you made, Sir, with respect to the drug problem and with respect to environment are timely and are of great importance to us. We know,
because we are not naive, that the terrible scourge of the drug problem is not just as a consequence of where the drugs are produced, but also as a consequence of those who use them. So your comments are timely and helpful.
Your comments with respect to the environment come at a time when at a global level and all around the earth people are more and more realizing that this may well be the great issue that we have to resolve. Your comments bring encouragement and help to your friends here.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It means a great deal to us, who share the continent with you, to hear your comments because leadership is something that in this day and age must go beyond national boundaries and that when you make these statements, which are the statements of a true leader, they are an inspiration for all of us. We are deeply grateful for the message that you have brought to us from your country.
In closing, Mr. President and Madam, let me say on behalf of all who are here today, and many who are not able to be here, we value immensely our friendship with your country. We want to continue the relationship in a more and more effective way. We welcome you here today. We wish you could stay longer. We wish both you and Madam and your colleagues the very warmest best wishes from all Canadians. Thank you.

Hear, hear.

Tuesday, April 9,1991
